work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: De centurione et contra Manichaeos et Apolinaristas

paragraphs.text: The clouds have whitened the earth with snow, and the snowflakes of the holy Scriptures whiten our souls with the divine word. For these enter into our souls, and like rain upon the grass and like snowfall upon the herbage, the divine snowflakes both water us and whiten us. They water us so that we bear the fruits of piety, and they whiten us by cleansing away the filth of sin; for whoever is washed by the divine word is shown to be whiter than snow, as David said: "You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow." Our soul is whitened both by the divine doctrines and by the moral precepts. Faith, which enlightens our mind, must go first, and works that make the soul shine must follow. Faith goes before all things, and the Savior marveled at it in the passages read today, saying: "Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith."

For the centurion grasped the dignity behind the miracles, asked the Savior for a command, and recognized his authority. The heretics, by contrast, though they read the Law and the Prophets and the Gospels and the apostles, failed to recognize his dignity and insulted the power of the Only-begotten. They say that he is subject to the Father's authority, not knowing that power belongs in common to the divine essence and that its authority is undivided: "For I and the Father are one." But let us return to our subject. That wonderful centurion says: "Say the word, and my servant will be healed. There is no need for you to come in the body. The divine power is everywhere. It is not confined by place, but encompasses all things by the divine Spirit. The Jews call you to a house, not knowing your dignity. But I know that you are present everywhere, that you command by a word and accomplish all things by a nod. I have entreated you as Master; I entreat you also as God. I implore you as Savior, and I appeal to you as benefactor. My servant lies at home, gravely stricken and in torment."

And see how robust the believer's mind is. He came not in person but through the elders. He was not shirking the task of making his plea; rather, he judged himself unworthy to be seen by the Savior. For he says: "I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. That is why I did not even consider myself worthy to come to you." Fine is the believer's modesty: out of reverence it declines to meet him face to face, yet through its true words it proclaims his dignity. The elders of the Jews came, elders of little faith pleading for a faithful servant. And the rulers of the synagogue said: "Come and heal him." But the centurion, recognizing his dignity, sent a delegation and said: "Do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you enter my house." "And how did you come to know the power of my word?"

"I know you are God from your miracles. The word of God brings nature into being and sets it right, and it is what gives substance to all visible things. Say the word, for 'By your word the heavens were made firm.' Say the word, for by a word you founded the earth, by a word you made the heavens firm, by a word you set bounds to the sea, by a word you set all things in order. You give commands to all your creatures: 'You send forth the light and it goes; you call it and it obeys you with trembling,' as Jeremiah says. 'And the stars shine for you with gladness. You called them and they said: Here we are.' You give orders to the visible creation and command the creation above the world. Can you not drive away diseases by that same command? Say the word. I need a word from God the Word. Say the word, and my servant will be healed." Now we must understand that there are great differences when it comes to faith. Listen to how it is, brother. Some reach the summit of faith, and others have a middling faith. Others are of little faith, others are of wavering faith, and others again are without faith.

Those who stand at the summit of faith are wonderful, like this centurion, to whom the Savior bore witness when he said: "Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith." Another is that Canaanite woman who approached him, whom the Lord admired and said: "O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish." These, then, are the ones whose faith is highest. The faithless are those wholly cut off from piety. Those of wavering faith stand on the border between faith and unbelief: at one moment they assent to the word, at another they draw back. The Gospel once charges the Savior's disciples with this kind of wavering, before they were made perfect. For when it was announced to them that the Lord had risen from the dead, some, it says, believed, but others doubted. To doubt means to stand with a divided heart, believing and disbelieving at once. The souls of many often suffer this when they think about Christ. For when we take on the heretics, the listeners at one moment assent to the dignity of the Only-begotten, but at another their minds are shaken by the heretics' words and they find themselves in doubt. At one moment they look to the glory of Christ; at another they turn aside to the wickedness of the heretics.

But God rebuked such littleness of faith, for faith of this kind falls short and is deficient. It is possible to believe, and yet to believe deficiently. That is why the apostle, knowing that faith can be deficient and lacking, says to the Romans: "So that when I come I may supply what is lacking in your faith." So it is possible both to believe and to fall short of the summit of faith. Littleness of faith, then, means thinking something small about God. The Savior reproaches Peter for this: he went out onto the sea and walked with faith, but afterward he doubted. That is why the Savior says to him: "You of little faith, why did you doubt?" He did not say "Faithless one," but "You of little faith," for Peter had shown some small faith. At first he saw the Savior walking on the sea, and the sea laying its waves beneath him and spreading out its back for the Master's steps. Then he called to mind the oracle of David which says: "Your way was in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints will not be known." So he says to his Savior: "Lord, if it is you, allow me to come to you on the waters."

The Lord gave permission, the servant followed, and a man stepped onto the back of the sea. Then the sea roused its waves. Or rather, a violent wind fell upon the waters, stirred up the sea's waves, and churned its whole surface. The servant was shaken and began to sink. His body was not the first thing in danger; it was his littleness of faith that plunged him under. He saw the sea raging and the winds in turmoil, abandoned his earlier faith, and was about to sink. And he calls on the Savior: "Lord, help me." And the Savior says to him: "You of little faith, why did you doubt?" And yet even his first words were not a matter of unbelief. To say "If it is you, command me to come on the waters" was the mark of one who recognized the dignity of the one giving the command. And as he was sinking, he looked to no one else but sought help from him and said, "Lord, help." That is the mark not of one who disbelieves but of one who believes. So the Gospel faults him not because he called on the Lord, but because he thought he was sinking while the Lord was present.

"Why," he says, "were you afraid of the sea after I had given you permission, after I had given the nod? I gave you leave and said 'Come,' and you thought the wind was stronger than my command? Did the wind frighten you, as if it were stronger than my nod? Am I not the one who walks on the wings of the winds? Does the sea terrify you? I am the one who threatens the sea and dries it up. Why then do you fear the creation when the Creator is present?" But perhaps Peter too will say: "Then why, Lord, did the sea dare to rebel while you were present? Why did it raise waves while you were present?" The sea rebelled, Peter, not out of contempt for Christ, but to test you. For the sea was always the tutor that corrected the disciples' unbelief.

On another occasion the Savior went out onto the sea, this time not on foot but by boat. For when he wishes, he makes his dignity known; when he wishes, he fulfills the dispensation. He walked on the sea as on solid ground; he went out in a boat as a man. And he not only boarded the boat but also slept in it. The nature that never sleeps slept in a boat? He who lulls the waves to sleep slept in a boat, he of whom the prophet said: "Behold, he who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep." He went aboard and slept, and again the sea raised its waves. It did not do so to show contempt for the Lord, but to expose the disciples' little faith. By little faith I mean the faith they had before they were made perfect. Let no one seize on my words. I am not accusing the apostles; I am exposing their weakness, so that afterward you may recognize their power. For Simon the fisherman is one thing and Peter the apostle another; Matthew the tax collector is one thing and Matthew the evangelist another.

First recognize how lowly the fishermen were, and then admire the greatness of the apostles. The sea raises its waves. They were in danger and tossed by the storm. And the one who rebukes the sea was there, yet he did not rebuke it. For he knew it to be a good tutor, training the disciples through danger. So they stood there and saw him sleeping like a man, and they plead with him as a man, saying: "Master, get up, save us, we are perishing!" You call him "Master"? That is why the sea is angry, and why it rebels against you: you do not yet recognize your Lord, but call him "Master," saying "Master!" So either take back that word, or I will not still the waves. "Master, we are perishing!" He who was called Master rises up and shows himself to be Lord. And what does he say to them? "Why are you afraid, you of little faith?" See how everywhere he rebukes the one who does not recognize his dignity. Why do you call him Master? "I saw you sleeping," one of them says, "and I came to you as to a man." Well then, because you saw him sleeping, you failed to recognize the dignity that never sleeps. Could you not say, as David did: "Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord?" Why did you not call him Lord, but Master, as though he were an ordinary teacher? If you call him Master, are you asking him for help? What master can lull the waves to sleep? What master can rebuke a storm at sea? If you think he is a master, let the master sleep. But if you call on him as God, recognize his dignity and receive his help.

He rebukes them for their little faith, but he gives orders to the sea by his authority. And he says to the sea: "Silence! Be still!" The moment the word went forth, the sea recognized the command. It was ordered to be silent, and it fell silent. It was ordered to be calm, and it did not object. It was this, I think, that blessed David was announcing in advance, or rather foretelling, when he said in the hundred and sixth psalm, sketching a picture of the apostles and the storm at sea: "Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do their work in many waters, they saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep." Sometimes one of our opponents carries the listener away by saying: "David is describing the wonders at the Red Sea, which the Israelites saw as they walked through the deep, when the waters congealed into a wall, when Pharaoh was drowned and Israel was saved. It was then," he says, "that those who went down saw the wonders in the deep." But the opening of the psalm refutes them. The sons of Israel went in on foot, whereas here he speaks not of those who walk but of those who sail. That is why he says: "Those who go down to the sea in ships." And the phrase "who do their work" signifies nothing other than the fishermen's craft. "Who do their work in many waters," that is, the fishermen, "they saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep."

What wonders? "He spoke, and the stormy wind arose." Here he shows that the sea was stirred up by God's command. It would not have raged against the disciples if the Lord had not willed it. "Its waves were lifted up." And what of the apostles? "They were troubled, they staggered like a drunkard, and all their wisdom was swallowed up." What wisdom? Their faith. Their wisdom was swallowed up, overpowered by little faith, "and they cried to the Lord in their distress": "Master, Master, we are perishing!" "And he saved them for his name's sake." And what came after this? That command in the Gospel: "Silence! Be still!" See how the prophet foretells it: "And he rebuked the storm, and it settled into a breeze, and its waves fell silent." So he rebukes the sea, and it grows calm. It recognized the Lord's command and is still. He rebuked it in order to calm it; he did not threaten it, so as not to dry it up. Had he threatened it, he would have dried it up, as the prophet says: "Threatening the sea and drying it up."

Then, after the rebuke, the disciples begin to say: "Who is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?" Note how they still did not recognize his dignity, because they were looking at the dispensation. Then what does the Gospel add? "Some of the disciples in the boat," it says, "came and worshiped him, saying: Truly you are the Son of God." See what good the sea did. Before the turmoil they called him Master; after the turmoil they confessed him as Son of God. The turmoil revealed his dignity: "Truly you are the Son of God." I have said all this to show the distinctions between faith, unbelief, little faith, and wavering faith. Now the Savior, extolling the centurion for saying "Say the word, and my servant will be healed," says to those following him: "Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith."

Did you not find faith in Israel? Were you not asked to lay your hand on Peter's mother-in-law? If they did not believe, how could they have pleaded with you? But he did not say "I have not found faith," but "I have not found such faith." "I was asked to lay my hand on Peter's mother-in-law, but no one was as clear-sighted as this man, to say: 'Say the word and drive away the fever.' Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, also called me and said to me: 'My little daughter is dying; come and heal her.' And when I said to him, 'Take heart, your daughter lives,' he said: 'Lord, come before she dies.' He did not recognize the dignity of my word, but demanded my bodily presence. Many believed, but not like this man; they believed, but not as he did. Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith."

So this believer brought out faith from the good treasure, but the heretic brings out unbelief from the evil treasure. And see the understanding of Scripture, or rather see what the fountain of wisdom utters: "The good man brings out good things from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings out evil things from the evil treasure of his heart." Notice how he has shown here not a nature that is evil or good, but free choice, which can incline toward this or look toward that. This saying refutes the wickedness of the Manichaeans, who declare that the flesh is evil and the soul comes from the good. For the children of the Manichaeans hold that the flesh belongs to the evil one, that is, the devil, and the soul to God.

But divine Scripture refutes them. If the heart belongs to the body, how does it bring out good things from an evil treasure? For what is evil by nature cannot bring out good things. Let them define it, then, however they like. They want our heart to be evil; then why does it bring out good things? Or is it good by nature? Either way you discover how rotten their unbelief is. That is why he set out both, speaking of an evil man and a good man, so that you would not attack nature but would recognize free choice. "The good man" comes first. See how he calls the nature good, or rather how he gives the designations "the good man" and "the evil man." If a man is evil by nature, why is he good? And if he is good by nature, why is he evil? See how he is not discussing nature here, but defining the power of free choice.

But the Manichaeans bring forward the apostle's text and twist his words, as if he said that the flesh is evil. "Listen," they say, "to what Paul teaches: 'The works of the flesh are plain: fornication, adultery,' and so on. 'But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace,' and so on. You see," they say, "how he sets flesh and spirit against each other, and calls the one a source of good things and the other a source of evil things." So let us see whether the apostle's words really agree with their wickedness, or whether they explain the power of free choice. If the flesh is an evil creation and the work of the evil one, why do good things come into being through the evil flesh? If the tongue were evil by nature, it ought not to speak of God. The tongue ought not to say words of blessing. The tongue ought to flee divine things altogether as foreign to it, and only speak obscenities and blasphemies and do everything proper to the flesh. How then does teaching about holiness come through the tongue, if it is of the nature of evil?

And why does God's word pass through these ears, which on their view are instruments of the devil? If the instrument is alien, how does it receive the working of the good? If the eyes are of the evil nature, why do they look up to him who dwells in heaven? If the mouth belongs to the evil one, why does the prophet say: "My mouth shall speak wisdom"? For wisdom is foreign to wickedness. If the hands are an evil instrument, why do they give alms? Why are they spread out to God? "For I stretch out my hands to God Most High, who made heaven and earth." If this belly that receives food were the handiwork of the evil one, why does it receive the law within it? "I desired to do your will, O God," he says, "and your law is within my belly." If the feet are a part of the evil one, why do they worship? For bending the knee in worship is done by means of the feet. And why does David say: "My foot has stood on level ground"? If it belongs to wickedness, how does it know uprightness? Let these points refute the impiety of the heretics.

What then does Paul mean when he says: "The works of the flesh are plain"? If, as you have shown, the whole body becomes an instrument of truth, of God's wisdom and goodness, why does Paul disparage the flesh? By "flesh" he means the mind set on the flesh: gratifying the flesh alone and not caring for the soul, providing for the present and neglecting the future. When someone indulges in luxury and busies himself with adorning his body so as to pamper it, while his soul is covered in countless festering wounds, then he is fleshly, because he is devoted to the flesh and takes no care for his soul. And to show that by "flesh" he means the mind set on the flesh, Paul says to the faithful: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." Were those he was writing to without flesh, then? The heretics do not know the idioms of the Scriptures; they are ignorant of how Scripture's thought fits together. If the flesh is foreign to God, why did God say: "It shall come to pass in the last days that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh"? Why not on every soul? Why not on every mind, but on all flesh? If the flesh is foreign to God, why does David say: "To you all flesh shall come"?

In fact, Scripture often calls the whole human being "flesh," naming the whole from a part. Often it calls the same human being "soul," again naming the whole from a part. And often it calls the whole human being "breath." When it chooses to call a human being "flesh," it names not only the body but also the soul, as in the verse we have already cited: "To you all flesh shall come," meaning every human being. For flesh on its own, without soul or mind, is not what is being announced. Again, when it wants to refer to the whole human being by the word "soul," it says: "Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy-five souls." Clearly those who went down into Egypt were not bodiless souls but complete human beings. And sometimes divine Scripture calls the whole human being "breath," as in: "Let every breath praise the Lord." Not only there, but also when King Jehu was slaying his enemies, the book of Kings says: "And King Jehu struck down the house of Ahab, and no breath was left in his house," meaning that no human being was left. So Scripture speaks of the flesh in one way when it is proclaiming our nature, and in another way when it is refuting the mind set on the flesh.

But let us return to our subject. "The works of the flesh are plain": not of the visible flesh, but of the mind set on the flesh. And so that you may learn that he is disparaging not this flesh of ours but an undisciplined mind, listen to him listing these things: "The works of the flesh are plain: fornication, adultery, idolatry." Grant that fornication and adultery belong to the body. Is idolatry a work of the body or a practice of the soul? "The works of the flesh are plain: fornication, adultery." Do these alone belong to the flesh, or also "idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, fits of rage, selfish rivalries, dissensions"? All these are foreign to the body and proper to the soul. I say they are proper to the soul, not by nature but by free choice. Indeed, if you pay close attention, you will find the heretics' own definition turned against them.

They say that the soul belongs to God but the flesh to the devil. Yet we find from Scripture that the flesh is counted worthy of the Holy Spirit, while the soul does not receive the things of the Spirit. I am speaking here of the wording, not saying that the soul is never counted worthy; I am opposing the heretics' argument. If the flesh is foreign to God, how did God say, “I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh”? If the soul is God's own work, why does the natural man, the man of the soul, not receive the things of the Spirit? It has therefore been clearly shown that the works of the flesh do not belong to the body, but to the fleshly mind. Paul explains this elsewhere too, when he says, “The mind of the flesh is hostile to God.” It is not the flesh that is hostile, but the mind of the flesh. Have you learned what “flesh” means? Hold this definition firm. And when Paul says that “flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God,” understand, he means, that the mind of the flesh does not inherit the kingdom of God. For the flesh is not excluded from the inheritance. It is those who deny the resurrection who make use of this saying.

“How,” he says, “can you say that the flesh is raised, when Paul says, ‘Flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God’?” Flesh, that is, the fleshly mind, does not inherit the kingdom; in other words, whoever thinks wicked things is a stranger to the kingdom. That is why the apostle, wishing elsewhere to explain what “Flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God” means, says in his letter to the Corinthians: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with men, nor drunkards, nor revilers will inherit the kingdom of God.” So when Paul often speaks of the flesh, he is not disparaging the visible form, but the fleshly mind. And how can the flesh be evil when it was counted worthy to become the temple of God the Word? Why would the Good One take up a work that was foreign to him, if what he had fashioned were not his own? Why does he take up what is foreign? Why does he set right what is foreign? Why does he heal the blind, and not let wickedness go lame? Wickedness, when blind, is powerless and shown to be weak. Let it stay weak! Why strengthen its instruments? But the creation is not foreign to him. Hear him say to the Pharisees: “Have you not read that he who made them made them male and female?” Male and female is not a shaping of souls, but of bodies.

These things also refute the heretics who bring a new drama before us, I mean the followers of Apollinaris, who say that the Savior took on an ensouled body without the mind. Listen to how they put it, for perhaps you do not know the new drama of this heresy. What do I mean? What do the heretics say? I do not come to this inquiry without reason. It is because a great uproar has been stirred up by certain people against the faith, as though they held right views and the Church were limping in the faith. So it is necessary to lay bare both the absurdity of that newly invented impiety and the steadfastness of the faith that does not shake the apostolic rule. The heretics say that God the Word took on an ensouled body without the mind. And if you ask them why he did not take on the mind, they say: “Because the first creation was corrupted and the devil deceived man, and man was deceived by surrendering his own mind to the devil; so he did not take it, lest it muddy the plan of salvation.” I do not know whether the listeners have not already condemned the heretics before the examination, but even so, let us test the question.

The heretics say that the Savior became man without the mind, and as evidence for their own view they drag in that saying of the Gospel, “The Word became flesh.” “It did not say,” he says, “that the Word became man, but flesh.” But it has been shown from what was said earlier that “flesh” in general signifies man: “To you all flesh shall come.” But let us ask why he did not take on the mind. “So that it would not hinder salvation.” So then, was he afraid of the mind, as being stronger and able to hinder the plan of salvation? If God the Word himself declined the mind, why am I judged? Why did he bind up with me so great an evil, which he himself declined? And why does he judge me for the sins I have committed?

But see another piece of their folly. “If there were the Word of God and a human mind,” he says, “there would be a battle.” But battles arise between equals, not between the lesser and the superior. If they said that the nature of the mind was equal in rank to the power of God the Word, they would rightly be bringing forward this equality, so that it would not cause strife. But if the one is God and the other a human faculty of thought, why do you cast out the mind? “So that it would not rebel,” he says, “against the plan of salvation.” Is there anything stronger than God? Is there anything that overcomes and limits his will? Paul overcame the mind—Paul, admittedly an ordinary man, admittedly having a human mind—and he says, “But we have the mind of Christ,” as though the human mind had been put to death and changed into a divine mind. And in Paul and the apostles the mind that thinks evil things was put to death and one mind took the place of another, yet in the divine body it was going to rebel against the Creator of nature? I remind those who know these things, and I speak to those who know, so that no one may unwittingly take in the venom of the heresy, and none of the simple may give up their ears to the deception.

“He did not take on the mind,” he says. Why? “Because it would have distorted and muddied the plan of salvation.” Then why did he take on this flesh too? For Paul does not say that sins are the works of the mind; he ascribed all sin to the flesh, not to the mind. “For the works of the flesh are plain,” he says, “which are fornication, adultery,” and the rest. Why then did he take on sinful flesh, if the flesh is opposed to the Spirit? For what reason did he take on what is opposed? But, you say, he quenched the resistance of the flesh and made it be still. Then did he not likewise make the mind be still? What folly, man! Wine changes the mind; does God not change the mind? But let the folly be laughed at, and let the things of God be proclaimed. There was, then, in the Savior's flesh the human mind, but it did not think human thoughts, just as the flesh did not either. The flesh was human, yet it surpassed human limits by the power that is above the world.

And so that I may hand you a clear and unconfused picture, take, I beg you, the proofs of what has been said with patience. In the flesh there are passions that lie outside sin, and there are passions that lie within sin. Likewise in the soul there are passions outside sin, and passions within sin. What do I mean? Passions of the flesh outside sin are hunger, thirst, and sleep. These are passions, but not of sin; they belong to the weakness of the flesh: hunger, thirst, sleep, growing weary from walking, and many other things akin to these. But there are other passions of the flesh: licentiousness, a lustful eye that looks wickedly and pries into other people's faces, a tongue that utters deceit, hands stretched out to do violence. These are works of sin. We shall find, then, that the Savior, in the flesh, was wholly and entirely above the passions that lead to sin, but came within the passions that show weakness, for the sake of the plan of salvation. For he hungered: “having fasted forty days, he was afterward hungry.” And being thirsty he asked the Samaritan woman for water, and having traveled he grew weary from the journey. The nature that knows no weariness grew weary; he who feeds all hungered; he who waters the world thirsted; he who lulls the waves to sleep slept. He displayed all the passions of the flesh, apart from sin. But the passions that lie within sin he did not commit, he of whom it is said, “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

You have seen him share in the passions of the flesh that are outside sin. Now see him share in the passions of the soul that are outside sin. Passions of the soul that are reckoned as sin are evil thoughts and shameful imaginings. These are passions of a soul that inclines toward sin by its own free choice. But the soul has other passions that are outside sin: grief, timidity, and fear. No one was ever condemned for being timid; no one was rejected for fear; no one was dishonored for grief. For these are common passions of nature, and the passions of the soul that are outside sin are blameless. Just as he shared [?] in the passions of the flesh that are outside sin, so he also shared in the passions of the soul that are outside sin. Hear him say: “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death,” and again, “My soul is troubled.” Trouble is the working of fear. The flesh, the human vessel, was afraid. It was afraid of the experience of death. He himself makes the distinction and clearly shows that it was not the divine Spirit that was timid, but the flesh that recognized its own weakness: “The spirit,” he says, “is willing, but the flesh is weak.” He grieved and was troubled.

Here pay close attention, you who say that there was no human mind in the Savior's flesh. He himself said that he both grieved and was troubled. Either grant the mind that is by nature troubled and grieved, or, if you cast it out and bring in God in place of the reasoning faculty, you attach these passions to God. For what is he saying? That without the mind the soul grieves and fears and is troubled? That is impossible. And I offer the proof from experience itself. Infants admittedly have both soul and body. The mind is present in them, but it has not yet become distinct. It exists, but it has not yet received its proper activity. And just as the tongue is born together with the child at once, yet the child has not yet received speech from nature, but the tongue is an instrument of speech and has no speech, so too the mind is implanted in the soul at once, but does not at once receive its activity. As time goes on, the mind is awakened and the tongue is trained. So while infants are in the condition of childhood and have not yet received a discerning mind, but have it lulled to sleep by inexperience and resting in simplicity, until then they neither fear what ought to be feared nor grieve over what ought to be grieved over; and even if they grieve or rejoice, both their grief and their gladness are without reasoning.

What do I mean? An infant can laugh on a day of mourning while others weep; it can ask for bread while everyone mourns. For it does not [?] reckon with what lies before it. It sees its father dead and does not reckon the calamity. It sees its mother laid out and is not struck by the grief that has befallen it; its simplicity leads it into freedom from care, and in mourning it is not troubled but laughs. And on the road, often, when robbers attack and bare their swords and everyone is in terror, the infant is not troubled, for it has no experience of sword and blood and murder. When it sees a snake it is not alarmed. It sees fire and is not afraid, but delights in its brightness and often puts its hand into the fire. Have you never seen an infant reach out its hand to the lamp, attending to its brightness and not considering its power to burn? And just as distressing things do not trouble it, so neither do bright things rouse it to gladness. An infant can cry and wail and complain on a wedding day, and, being without reasoning, shares neither in the joy nor in the grief. Since, then, you cast the mind out of the human vessel that the Savior took on, either give me this mind that grieves, or, by casting it out, you plainly bring in a Godhead that grieves and is troubled.

I would have prayed that none of you should hear either their teachings or the explanations about them, for I did not want you to see either the wound or the plaster for the wound. But since the sore is spreading, and under the guise of orthodoxy it brings in false doctrine and says that Christ did not take on a mind, and makes innovations against the apostolic teachings, we have of necessity examined these things, so that we might both silence them and make you secure. Receive the authoritative teaching of the faith. Learn that Christ took on the whole man who had fallen, and that he restored [?] the whole nature that had been undone. Did the flesh alone sin? Did the soul alone sin? Was the mind alone a stranger to sin? If the mind had no share in sin, it would not have needed healing either. “For those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” But if the mind too had a share in sin, why do you bring in a partial healing? The soul sinned and needed healing. Indeed it is written: “The soul that sins shall die.” And see the precision: the sin that Scripture ascribed here to the soul, it elsewhere reckons to the flesh, accusing flesh and understanding together, so that no one might think that the flesh is in itself an evil creation, while the mind is a stranger to the flesh and free of sins. The inspired apostle declares it clearly, saying something like this: “And we were by nature children of wrath, doing the wishes of the flesh and of the thoughts,” in order to show clearly that soul and body and mind all sinned. And that it is not the flesh alone that suffers corruption, but the mind too, he says again elsewhere: “Men corrupted in mind.” If, then, the flesh sinned and the soul sinned and the mind was corrupted, and the whole vessel was corrupted, why would he not take on the whole?

“But if you speak of a complete man,” he says, “you have your hopes placed in a man.” I proclaim Christ as man and do not deny it—but man and God: God by his dignity, man by the plan of salvation. I call him man because of the condition visible outwardly, God because of the dignity within, dwelling in the humanity as in a temple. And I do not refuse to say “man,” since Paul did not deny it either: “For there is one mediator between God and men,” he says, “the man Jesus Christ.” And do you want to learn precisely that the Lord calls himself Son of Man? Hear him say: “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” If he did not truly take on the image of man which the devil had corrupted, why does he call a half-man “Son of Man”? And why, brother, if he did not have the mind, but the visible instrument consisted only of soul and body, why does the apostle call the Savior Adam? For if he is not complete, he is not Adam. The apostle names our Lord Jesus God because of his dignity: “Christ according to the flesh,” he says, “who is God over all, blessed.” And he calls him man because of the plan of salvation. And he names him Adam in order to show the plan of salvation: “The first man Adam,” he says, “became a living soul; the second Adam a life-giving spirit.” If he did not clothe himself with the whole Adam, why is he called Adam?

And so that you may learn again from another clear proof, brother, that the whole man was taken up through the Lord's flesh, hear Paul say: “Knowing this, that our old man was crucified.” If it was not the whole man, why does he call him the old man? But let this suffice against the heretics. Let us return to our own nobility. Our nobility is the apostolic faith, the apostolic profession. We all have the mind of Christ. But those who deny the mind are “men corrupted in mind, disqualified regarding the faith.” But so much for these things. May we, abiding by the apostolic definitions, keep our praise of God undefiled, wall off our ears from the heretics, and know the mind of the Church, know the profession of the faith, know the mystery of baptism, and know the dignity of the faith. And may we be counted worthy of the faith, so that as we were baptized, so we may also believe and so give glory, offering true glory to the Father and to the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
